Q: Java Spring MySql8 thread safe select then delete A:

Let's, hypothetically, say that you managed to do this task; your plan works as designed, and it either all happens or none of it happens, guaranteed, with safety that no two systems/threads could ever touch the same rows.

What happens when immediately_ after the DB has committed this update, and the ids are midflight from the DB to your app or in your JVM, being processed,

DISASTER! .... someone trips over a powercable or something and the JVM is hardkilled?

The rows have already been deleted and that has already been committed!

The system's completely failed now. Some job had to be done, it wasn't done, but the DB state says that it was done.

(Perhaps you say: Ah, it's okay, this is an optional job: Allright, much easier implementation: Put on a 1 second clock: TRUNCATE table_name CASCADE; and never do anything, Voila! Simple, easily maintained, highly performant, and fits the spec, what's not to like?)

The entire model is presumably wrong; it's hard to imagine this can ever be right.

Generally all such stuff boils down into one of two generalized concepts:

  • Every single last observable part of this entire operation is all happening in a single database.

It can involve a great many steps, it can bounce between a JVM and a DB engine multiple times, with much of the calculations done on the JVM side, that's all fine, as long as every actual effect that this process causes is 100% in terms of DB operations. For example, the job is 'query a database to find all adults, then for each account ping the insurer's API to check they are still insured, and then store in the DB for each person-row that they are insured or not, and the timestamp of this latest check'. The key here is that all storage is in the DB, and every action outside of it is repeatable and effect-free. For example, if you've done all this work and juuust before the actual storing of 'I just checked the insurance status of this person and they are insured' someone trips over a power cable - no problem. Reboot the box, and it'll repeat the operation. Unless for some reason you may only ask for insurance info just the one time ever (and that would be state observable outside the DB), this is fine. At worst you've now called the insurer's API twice for the same person, but it really isn't superfluous - you made the call and before you managed to store the result of it, someone trips over a power cable. Nothing you can do to stop that.

So what's the solution? Do it all in a single transaction and make sure you have the right isolation level. MySQL is notorious for sucking at it, so if this is your situation you'd have to ask a follow up question or ask someone else because all I know about MySQL is that it's a bit weird in such regards.

On most DB systems (including postgres), it's a simple matter of using the SERIALIZABLE transaction isolation level. There is no need to fuss with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED. Just do your stuff, all in one transaction, commit at the end, and do what a retry exception tells you to do (namely, start over, the whole thing. Good DB abstractions take care of this for you, but it does mean all your in-transaction code must be idempotent: Running it multiple times must have the same effect as running it once).

  • Not a single operation: There's observable state change outside of the DB, or its an operation on multiple DBs

In this case things get dicey - there is no way to do this in a simple fashion. You can't transaction across boundaries like this. There is no one answer; it depends on the process you are designing.

But there is a general 'formula' to how to derive at the right answer that works for virtually all such situations: Use a concept called journalling. Instead of:

  1. Do the thing

You do:

  1. Register that we're about to 'do the thing', and wait for whatever system registers this to report that it is definitely safely stored (e.g. commit your transaction, flush your disks, wait for a pingback from follow-mode live DB copies, and so on).

  2. do the thing, in a way that one can confirm that the thing has been done later if needed, and in a way that is atomic (it entirely succeeds or entirely fails) or which consists of separate atomic steps that can all be individually verified.

  3. Log that you've done the thing.

Then you combine the above procedure with a boot cleanup: Upon application startup, the app checks the log and fixes any dangling issues. If during boot you see a registration of 'about to do the thing' but you do not see a registration that 'I completed the thing', then one of two things has happened:

  • The thing has been done, but something crashed before registering that the thing has now been done.

  • The thing has not been done.

Use the verification to check, and update accordingly. If it's a multi-step process, finish it or undo the half-baked process (reverse all steps you can verify have been completed). Afterwards we're back in atomic state: The thing happened (and continue accordingly; you may even delete the log, though they can often be useful to keep around), or the thing did not happen in any way, and continue as if it never did. Perhaps do it now.

Here's an example of an ATM, which is of the second kind: Most banking stuff is DB based, but that cassette of bills and the hopper thing that spits them out isn't a database and therefore cannot operate within the confines of a DB transaction.

  1. User enters card, types in PIN, indicates they want to withdraw €300,-.

  2. Start transaction.

  3. Check that user has 300 to withdraw. Also check that the camera is currently functioning (there's a camera pointed at the general room and the hopper). If not, it ends here, show an error message on the ATM machine, commit, and end.

  4. (If we get here, the user has 300 to withdraw).

  5. prepare the hopper to store €300 in bills.

  6. Register in the DB that the little door thing is about to be opened for the customer (this is the 'I'm about to do X' part), and commit.

  7. Tell the actual machine to open the door. Wait for the user to take it.

  8. (Action: User either retrieves the cash and the machine detects this, or, the user waits to long and the machine draws the bills back in and puts it into the process-later pile).

  9. Start transaction, and finish the log of the 'about to open the door with the bills': Either register that the bills have been taken back, or that the user has taken them. Commit.

That's the end of the process.

This process is crash proof. The worst places for a power outage to throw a spanner in the works is if the system goes down immediately after committing "I am about to open the door".

If that happens, and the power is restored, the ATM boots up and notices that the last thing it remembers is that it was about to open the door. It may have opened it, or the power may have gone out before it opened.

At that point the ATM (which has its own 'open door' log) checks if it knows for sure it never opened the door, in which case it redirects the bills to the check-later pile and adds the €300,- back to the user's account. The user can now just redo the operation if it was a short power outage. If the door has been opened, the ATM now simply cannot tell anymore, and we've hit a real problem. Except, the cameras presumably might help, and the system logs that a human operator will have to check the fate of the bills. Until an operator clears the situation the user's account is deemed to have €300 in limbo and will not have those available for normal banking ops.

Here even in a terrible situation (real mechanical doors and random humans slightly incentivized to screw with the system - that's a pretty terrible place to be when wanting to design safe, atomic systems!), the recovery process is easy and difficult to abuse.

And the power lies in that 'I am about to do the thing' 'do the thing' 'register that I have done the thing' process.

NB: A good example of the journalling concept is file systems. In the past, yoinking the power cable of a computer would risk disk corruption, and a pricey check operation would have to be performed; even if you run it, data may be gone, even data that the system at the time reported as having been safely stored on disk.

But that's all in the past: Modern systems use journalling and you can just hard-cycle the power, there is no need for a lengthy 'disk check' once you reboot, data is never in a fantom zone (where the system reports to an app it has been stored, but then it wasn't): The worst case scenario is that the disk is just fried entirely; nothing a file system can do about that. They do this by journalling. "Disk check at boot" is now simply: Check the journal, finish the job, boot as normal.

Q: FTP The remote server returned an error: (530) Not logged in A:

You can supply the user name and password on the FTP URL. For example, if you want to download /path/filename from ftp://ftp.foo.com, you can encode the user name and password like this:

ftp://username:password@ftp.foo.com/path/filename

You should be able to construct such a URL for the file you're trying to download. Then pass that URL to XDocument.Load.

Note, however, that the password is sent in the clear (i.e. no encryption, etc.).

See Section 3.2 of RFC 1738 for more info.
